# Transing the Frame: Middle Eastern and North African Cinema, Gendered Recognition, and Transnational Representation

Films with transgender themes from the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) form a dispersed, transnational field rather than a single regional movement. The best-documented bodies of work are Iranian and Turkish: Iranian films repeatedly stage the conflict between self-recognition, religious authorization, medical diagnosis, and legal legibility, while Turkish documentaries more often connect trans life to activism, urban violence, labor, displacement, and collective organizing. *Facing Mirrors* (Negar Azarbayjani, Iran, 2011), *Be Like Others* (Tanaz Eshaghian, Iran, 2008), and *Trans X Istanbul* (Maria Binder, Turkey, 2014) demonstrate three distinct representational formations: a fictional cross-class friendship organized around mobility and family pressure; a clinic-centered documentary about medicalization and citizenship; and an activist documentary about structural violence and transnational collaboration.

The evidence is considerably thinner for Egypt, Lebanon, the Gulf, Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, and Hebrew-language cinema. Those contexts nevertheless matter, both because they contain adjacent representations that must not be misclassified as transgender and because diasporic films complicate the boundaries of national cinema. A careful account must therefore distinguish transgender identity from drag, cross-dressing, intersex embodiment, gay and lesbian representation, and temporary gender passing, while also recognizing that local terms and institutions do not map neatly onto Anglophone categories.

This paper first defines MENA and establishes a deliberately bounded corpus. It then surveys historical, industrial, and regional contexts; develops a framework from trans theory and film theory; and offers close readings of the three principal films. The final comparison examines medicalization, recognition, agency, class, religion, nationality, language, documentary ethics, censorship, festival circulation, and the politics of the transnational gaze.

## Scope, terminology, and corpus

### What “MENA” means here

“MENA” is not a natural or culturally uniform geographical unit. It is a strategic scholarly designation for a region shaped by overlapping linguistic, ethnic, racial, religious, colonial, and migratory histories. The term may include North Africa, the Arab Mashriq, Iran, Turkey, Israel/Palestine, and—depending on the institutional context—the Gulf. Its boundaries are disputed, and its history is inseparable from European imperial classification. A recent transnational feminist account of MENA film and media retains the term precisely while acknowledging this colonial inheritance: it emphasizes interconnected histories and solidarities without treating the region as homogeneous ([“Transnational feminist approaches to film and media from the Middle East and North Africa”](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/25785273.2023.2231775)).

This paper uses MENA in that critical and provisional sense. It includes films made in the region, films produced through regional and European or North American partnerships, and diasporic films about MENA subjects whose production, financing, language, or circulation crosses national borders. Turkey is included because Turkish cinema is deeply connected to Middle Eastern, Mediterranean, European, and transnational film cultures, and because the principal Turkish case study belongs to a collaborative German-Turkish production context. Israel/Palestine is treated as a contested and internally differentiated field rather than a single national cinema. The Maghreb is used in its more specific sense of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia, especially where scholarship distinguishes it from the Mashriq.

National cinema remains useful for identifying institutions, languages, censorship regimes, and production histories, but it is insufficient as the sole framework. Yaron Shemer’s account of the “cinemas” of the Middle East and North Africa stresses both internal differences and shared regional tendencies in discourse, aesthetics, production, and distribution ([Shemer’s course framework](https://ncmideast.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/1065/2011/02/cinema-of-Middle-East-and-North-Africa.pdf)). Andrew Higson’s transnational model similarly directs attention to cross-border production, circulation, and reception. Alexander De Man argues that “diaspora cinema” is most useful as a critical and heuristic framework rather than as a fixed category based on the ethnicity of filmmakers or the presumed authenticity of their subjects ([De Man, “Reframing Diaspora Cinema”](https://www.alphavillejournal.com/Issue25/HTML/ArticleDeMan.html)).

### Corpus rule

The primary inclusion rule is explicit transgender identification or a clearly documented transgender theme. A film belongs in the core corpus when one or more of the following is present:

- a character or documentary subject identifies as transgender or transsexual;
- the film centers gender transition, gender-affirming medical care, or trans-specific legal recognition;
- the film’s subject is trans activism, trans community formation, or structural violence against trans people;
- a scholarly source explicitly identifies the film as transgender or gender-nonconforming representation.

This rule deliberately excludes films whose only relevant material is same-sex desire, gender nonconformity, drag performance, or cross-dressing. Such films remain important comparative or boundary cases, because they show how MENA cinemas have historically made gender and sexuality visible, but they do not establish transgender identity by themselves.

| Film or project | Place and date | Form and transgender relevance | Status in this paper |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Facing Mirrors* | Iran, 2011; theatrical release in Iran in 2012 | Fictional feature about Adineh/Eddy, a trans man seeking to leave Iran for surgery | Principal case study |
| *Be Like Others* | Iran, 2008; some secondary records list 2007 | Documentary about Iranian trans people navigating psychiatric, medical, religious, and legal institutions | Principal case study |
| *Trans X Istanbul* | Turkey, 2014 | Documentary centered on activist Ebru Kırancı and trans struggles against hate crimes, displacement, and urban redevelopment | Principal case study |
| *Melting Away* | Israel, 2011 | Fictional family drama about Anna, a trans young woman, and her parents | Contextual direct case |
| *Cinema Fouad* | Lebanese television production, 1993 | Documentary treated by Jagger as a record of transgender and gender-nonconforming Palestinians in diaspora | Diasporic context |
| *Sultana’s Reign* | 2023 | Documentary treated by Jagger as a later representation of transgender and gender-nonconforming Palestinians in diaspora | Diasporic context |

The table is not a claim to exhaustiveness. The retrieved scholarship does not provide a complete, verified corpus covering every MENA country through September 2026. In particular, film-specific evidence remains insufficient for the Gulf, Egypt, Lebanon, much of North Africa, and Hebrew-language trans cinema. The absence of a retrieved title from those areas should therefore be read as a limit of the evidence assembled here, not as proof that no relevant films exist.

### Transgender, transsexual, drag, cross-dressing, intersex, gay, and lesbian

“Transgender” is used here as a broad contemporary umbrella for people whose gender differs from the sex assigned to them, including people who may or may not pursue hormones, surgery, legal transition, or binary identification. “Transsexual” is retained when discussing historical medical and legal vocabularies, local usage, or sources that use the term. It should not be treated as a universal or timeless synonym for transgender.

The distinction matters especially in Iran. In Persian, *tarajinsi* is described by interviewees as a relatively new term for transsexuality and, in some accounts, for a person willing to undergo sex-change surgery. *Tarajinsiyati* is a newer and broader term associated with transgender identity, desire, pleasure, and attraction. The relationship between the terms is unsettled: some interviewees understand *tarajinsi* as one form of *tarajinsiyati*, while others use them interchangeably ([Saeidzadeh, “Transsexuality in Contemporary Iran”](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10691-016-9332-x.pdf?error=cookies_not_supported&code=ea50af1c-567e-4583-a99a-13d40041f8dd)). Another study identifies *Amali Tasdigi Jinsiyat* as a recent Persian expression for surgery that changes the body or biological sex in order to affirm gender; the phrase itself suggests that the body changes rather than gender ([Azadi and Saeidzadeh](https://doi.org/10.1080/09589236.2022.2068517)).

Other Persian terms have different histories and meanings. *Dujinsi*, literally “a person with two sexes,” has been used at different moments for bisexual, transsexual, transgender, and intersex people, although Tehran surgeons interviewed by Saeidzadeh said that it increasingly referred to an intersex or “hermaphrodite” person. *Hamjinsbaaz* and *hamjinsgaraa* concern same-sex activity, desire, or sociality rather than gender identity. The distinction between gender and sexuality is therefore not merely a matter of translating English vocabulary into Persian; it is a question of institutional history and social power.

Drag is a performance practice, often involving stylized or theatrical gender presentation. A drag performer may be cisgender, transgender, nonbinary, or otherwise gender-nonconforming. Cross-dressing describes clothing or presentation that a culture codes as belonging to another gender; it does not establish a person’s identity. Iranian cinema’s early cross-dressing comedies, Egyptian films such as *Sukkar Hanem*, and the drag-club employment of Anna in *Melting Away* must not automatically be counted as transgender representations. In *Melting Away*, the character’s gender identity and her work as a performer are related but not identical: the film reveals Anna as transgender while also placing her in a drag-club environment ([Fox, “Israeli film embraces transgender teen”](https://jweekly.com/2013/06/21/israeli-film-embraces-transgender-teen-stunned-parents/)).

Intersex refers to variations in sex characteristics, not necessarily to a transgender identity. This distinction is historically important in Iran, where early surgical cases and legal discussions often concerned intersex bodies. Gay and lesbian describe sexual orientation or same-sex desire, not gender identity. *Caramel*, *Circumstance*, and *In Between* are valuable films about lesbian representation and queer visibility, but the scholarship supplied for this paper does not establish their protagonists as transgender.

Arabic and Hebrew terminology is less fully documented in the available evidence than Persian terminology. The Arabic term *shaadh* appears in discussions of Arab media as a stigmatizing term meaning “queer,” “pervert,” or “deviant,” but it is not a precise trans identity category. The evidence assembled here does not support a comparable, consistent account of Arabic or Hebrew trans vocabulary. That gap is itself significant: translation can make a region appear linguistically legible while obscuring the unstable, classed, religious, and locally situated meanings through which gender is lived.

## Historical and institutional contexts

### Iran: from gender disguise to medico-legal legibility

Iran offers the most extensively documented national context in this corpus, but it is also the one most likely to be reduced to a misleading paradox: the Islamic Republic permits gender-affirming surgery while criminalizing male same-sex sexual acts. That paradox is real, but it does not mean that Iran has either a simple policy of trans liberation or a single policy of forced transition.

The history is layered. Saeidzadeh’s socio-legal account traces reports of surgery for congenital intersex conditions to the Iranian press in the 1930s. The medical language of Gender Identity Disorder entered Iran in the 1960s, and the first officially reported non-intersex surgeries appeared in 1973 in Tehran and Shiraz. Iran’s Medical Association limited surgery to intersex cases in 1976. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini’s early jurisprudential writing on the permissibility of sex change dates to the 1960s, with sources variously identifying 1964 or 1967 as the date of the relevant text.

After the 1979 revolution, the legal-medical arrangement changed again. Some sources date a renewed fatwa or confirmation to 1982; others describe a 1984–85 process of judicial and medical regulation; journalistic accounts often date the “legalization” of transsexuality to 1987. These dates refer to different events: a jurisprudential text, a personal religious ruling, administrative implementation, government policy, and the later circulation of a judicial or legal interpretation. They should not be collapsed into one moment. Saeidzadeh explicitly argues that surgery was authorized through Islamic jurisprudence and institutional cooperation with medicine rather than through a clear statute recognizing transgender identity ([Saeidzadeh, 2016](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10691-016-9332-x.pdf?error=cookies_not_supported&code=ea50af1c-567e-4583-a99a-13d40041f8dd)).

Maryam Khatoon Molkara’s activism was central to this transition. According to the available accounts, Molkara repeatedly petitioned Khomeini and eventually received a ruling permitting surgery when approved by a reliable doctor. The state later developed a process involving psychiatric assessment, the Legal Medicine Organization, and judicial authorization. This history contradicts two common simplifications. First, the policy was not simply imposed from above; trans activism helped produce it. Second, religious authorization did not automatically create substantive legal equality or social acceptance.

Iranian cinema registers these shifts before and after the revolution. Kaveh Bassiri’s overview identifies late-1950s and 1960s cross-dressing films as a site of transgender discourse and names *Shahbaji Khanom* (1958) as a milestone. It also distinguishes the common patterns of male-to-female roles associated with comedy and trickery from female-to-male characters associated with coercion and struggles over women’s rights, citing *Madmazel Khaleh* (1957) and *Dokhtari be nam-e Tondar* (2000) ([Bassiri, “Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema”](https://www.academia.edu/38285158/Transgender_Identity_in_Iranian_Cinema)). These examples should be read historically rather than retroactively classified as straightforward trans narratives. A comic disguise and a trans character may both disturb gender norms while producing very different claims about identity.

Documentary attention intensified in the early 2000s. Bassiri identifies *Juste une femme* (2002), *Inside Out* (2005), *The Birthday* (2006), and *Be Like Others* as part of a period in which documentaries combined personal narratives with social critique and advocacy. The same overview notes criticism that some documentaries exoticized or oversimplified Iranian trans experience. Elhum Shakerifar’s work, as summarized by Saeidzadeh, similarly warns that Iranian trans people can be represented either as oppressed objects forced into surgery or as exotic objects of Western inquiry.

*Facing Mirrors* marked a different development: it brought a trans man into Iranian narrative cinema through a story of family, debt, mobility, and friendship. Its release created a public opening. The Guardian reported that the Tehran theatrical release in 2012 encouraged state television and radio to discuss transsexuality, a topic they had generally avoided. The producer also reported that young trans viewers encouraged others to see the film ([The Guardian, “Iranian film shines spotlight on taboo subject”](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2012/nov/02/iranian-film-taboo-subject-transsexuals)).

### Turkey: spectacle, censorship, and activist documentary

Turkish cinema has a different institutional history. The Yeşilçam industry, often called “Turkish Hollywood,” was active from the early 1950s to the late 1980s. Its decline closed production companies even as theatres remained important sites of exhibition; many of those theatres were later demolished or closed. This history matters because queer and trans representation developed through a changing relation between commercial melodrama, popular stardom, censorship, and independent activism.

Murat Akser’s historical overview argues that representations of sexuality outside heterosexual norms were consistently subjected to state censorship and negative media criticism, even as filmmakers became more daring from the mid-1960s onward. The period from 1962 to the present, in his account, moves through changing representations of lesbian, transsexual, and gay male characters ([Akser, “Changing LGBT Narratives in Turkish Cinema”](https://www.academia.edu/27805853/Changing_LGBT_Narratives_in_Turkish_Cinema)). The history is not a linear progress narrative. Saruhan’s study of three Turkish films from the 2000s concludes that even sympathetic films often reproduce stereotypes linking transsexuality to prostitution, alienation, psychological distress, and physical violence, while failing to empower characters or punish those who harm them ([Saruhan, “Transexuality in Turkey”](https://www.academia.edu/6368123/Transexuality_in_Turkey_The_Representation_of_Transexual_Identities_in_Contemporary_Turkish_Films)).

Bülent Ersoy’s public career makes the relationship between spectacle and law particularly visible. Her male-to-female transition coincided with the 1980 military coup; the regime banned her public performances and refused to recognize her gender status. Ertür and Lebow read *The End of Fame* (1981), now described as nearly lost, alongside Ersoy’s legal troubles. They call attention to the encounter between the “law of spectacle” and the “spectacle of law”: the stage produces gendered visibility, while the state attempts to regulate the juridical meaning of that visibility ([Ertür and Lebow, “Coup de Genre”](https://eprints.bbk.ac.uk/id/eprint/9473)).

The most significant shift for this paper is the emergence of documentary activism in the 2000s and 2010s. Cüneyt Çakırlar examines *Proudly Trans in Turkey* (Gabrielle Le Roux, 2012), *My Child* (Can Candan, 2013), and *Trans X Istanbul* as “screen activism.” These projects make activist spaces visible while reflecting on their own circulation, spectatorship, ethnographic address, and documentary form. Their politics are therefore inseparable from how they reach audiences and from how international funding translates regional activism into globally legible narratives ([Çakırlar, “Transnational Pride, Global Closets and Regional Formations of Screen Activism”](https://doi.org/10.1080/02560046.2017.1345966)).

Turkey’s exhibition infrastructure also reveals the importance of alternatives to conventional theatrical distribution. Başka Cinema, launched in November 2013 with the motto “festival all year long,” used nine theatres in Istanbul and four in other Turkish cities to exhibit alternative films. This kind of network does not guarantee access for trans films, but it demonstrates how alternative circulation can operate alongside or around commercial exhibition. The public-space restrictions documented in Istanbul show that exhibition itself can be regulated even when the content of a film is not directly censored.

### Israel, Palestine, and diasporic screen cultures

Israeli and Palestinian cases demonstrate why “national cinema” must be combined with diaspora and occupation studies. *Melting Away* (Doron Eran, 2011) is an Israeli family drama about Anna, a trans young woman whose parents rejected her after finding women’s clothing. When her father develops terminal cancer, her mother hires a detective to find her. The film reveals Anna’s identity within its first fifteen minutes and makes the parents’ gradual adjustment, rather than Anna’s identity, the central narrative problem. The critic Michael Fox emphasizes that the film treats parental recognition as the parents’ responsibility and refuses to make Anna’s gender a sensational twist ([Fox](https://jweekly.com/2013/06/21/israeli-film-embraces-transgender-teen-stunned-parents/)).

The film’s production context was shaped by the 2009 shooting at the Israel Gay Youth Organization in Tel Aviv, which killed two people. Its reception evidence is mainly journalistic and festival-based: it played at Frameline and other festivals, where program notes described it as an emotionally affecting story of family rejection, violence, and emerging acceptance. A festival synopsis also identifies Anna’s work as a performer in a trans club. Again, employment in drag performance should not be confused with the film’s representation of her as transgender.

Palestinian trans and gender-nonconforming representation is more explicitly diasporic. Aaron Jagger compares Mohamed Soueid’s *Cinema Fouad* (1993), a Télé Liban production, with Hadi Moussally’s *Sultana’s Reign* (2023), arguing that the two documentaries, made twenty years apart, trace changing diasporic experiences of transgender and gender-nonconforming Palestinians. Jagger places queer/trans theory alongside postcolonial and decolonial theory, especially Butler, Naficy, and Walter Mignolo, and emphasizes language, assimilation, nuance, and the need for a more expansive account of non-Western queerness ([Jagger, “Tracing the Diasporic Experiences…”](https://doi.org/10.1386/fm_00415_1)). The full article was not available in the supplied record, so the comparison can establish the corpus and its theoretical stakes but not support detailed shot-by-shot analysis.

*In Between* (Maysaloun Hamoud, 2016) belongs to the adjacent lesbian corpus rather than the trans corpus. Its representation of Palestinian women in Tel Aviv is nonetheless useful for understanding the politics of regional visibility. Maria Abdel Karim reads the film alongside *Caramel* and *Circumstance* through framing, lighting, performance, and spectatorship. The article also discusses the competing claims of Israeli LGBTQ branding, Palestinian queer vulnerability, occupation, and “pinkwashing” ([Abdel Karim](https://doi.org/10.33178/alpha.20.06)). These debates caution against treating Israel as simply a liberal refuge or Palestinian society as a single source of homophobia. Queer Palestinians can be subjected to patriarchal and religious pressure within Palestinian communities, state violence and occupation, and instrumental representations of LGBTQ rights by the Israeli state.

### The Maghreb, Arab cinema, and the evidentiary gap

The retrieved evidence supports a strong account of Maghrebi transnational cinema, but not a complete catalog of Maghrebi transgender films. Scholarship on North African cinema emphasizes the relationship between internal cultural politics and an “outside” that includes France, the former colonial power, and globalizing cultural and political forces. These forces can enable production through funding and circulation while also restricting it through market expectations and external representations ([Khalil and Dwyer](https://www.africabib.org/rec.php?RID=305275747)).

Kaya Davies Hayon’s study of the body in contemporary Maghrebi film includes eleven films from the Maghreb, France, and Switzerland. Its queer chapter treats *L’armée du salut* (Abdellah Taïa, 2014), *Tarik el hob* (Rémi Lange, 2001), and *Un fils* (Amal Bedjaoui, 2003) as representations of male same-sex desire, not transgender identity ([Petty’s review](https://doi.org/10.33178/alpha.20.23)). These films are important for theorizing embodiment and sexual desire, but they do not belong in a trans catalog without additional evidence.

Algerian cultural production offers a particularly instructive boundary. Chantal Zabus examines Marie-Pierre Pruvot’s *Marie parce que c’est joli* (2007) and Fériel Assima’s *Rouhlem ou le sexe des anges* (1996) as two Algerian key-texts involving transgender and intersex figures. The texts connect gendered embodiment to the colonial period and the Black Decade, and Zabus reads the protagonists’ bodies-in-transition as a metaphorical “transing” of the Algerian nation-state ([Zabus](https://doi.org/10.4312/an.52.1-2.69-96)). Because the supplied record describes these as textual works rather than films, they are comparative context rather than entries in the filmography.

Tunisia similarly appears in the evidence through literature rather than cinema. Charlotte Pardey compares *Hurlement* (Alia Mabrouk, 1992) and *Ṭurshqāna* (Masʾūda Bū Bakr, 1999), two novels with transgender themes. Her discussion shows how gender-affirming surgery, embodiment, and literary distribution were negotiated under Tunisian censorship, but the censorship evidence concerns books rather than film ([Pardey](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/full/10.3366/ccs.2024.0517)).

Merzak Allouache’s *Chouchou* (2003) supplies a more direct filmic example. Quinan describes its protagonist as a North African, female-identified, male-bodied migrant who arrives in France and begins to present and identify as a woman. The film’s comedy, migrant setting, and optimistic ending distinguish it from the Iranian and Turkish cases. It is a transnational European postcolonial film about a North African subject rather than a film produced entirely within a Maghrebi national cinema ([Quinan](https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/414515)).

For Egypt and Lebanon, the available evidence is stronger for coded queer representation, cross-dressing, and lesbian narratives than for explicitly transgender characters. Sari Bazz’s account of male-to-female cross-dressing in Arabic cinema identifies *Sukkar Hanem* (1960) as a comedy in which a failed actor remains in women’s clothing and mannerisms until the disguise is revealed as “a joke and an act.” The film is therefore a useful example of performance and heteronormative restoration, not evidence of a trans protagonist ([Bazz](https://wp.mykalimag.com/en/2021/02/18/men-dressed-as-women-cross-dressing-in-arabic-cinema/)).

No comparable, film-specific evidence was retrieved for the Gulf states. Nor is there enough evidence here to construct a verified Arabic- or Hebrew-language chronology of trans cinema. Those fields require further archival and language-specific work, but this paper preserves the underlying comparison by marking them as unavailable rather than treating silence as absence.

### Censorship, funding, distribution, and reception

MENA films with trans themes are shaped by several overlapping systems of control and circulation. These include state censorship, religious authority, family surveillance, medical gatekeeping, commercial distribution, international co-production, festival programming, activist networks, and digital platforms. The same transnational circuits that make films visible can also reshape their meanings.

Iranian cinema’s international visibility expanded during the 1990s through festival circulation. Research summarized by the Film Festival Research Network connects Iranian cinema’s international rise to censorship, international financing, festival programming, and political negotiations through cultural exchange. The same regional festival infrastructure grew through events such as Dubai International Film Festival, the Dubai Film Market, the Middle East International Film Festival in Abu Dhabi, and the Doha Tribeca Film Festival ([Film Festival Research Network bibliography](http://www.filmfestivalresearch.org/index.php/ffrn-bibliography/6-transnational-cinemas/6-4-the-middle-east/)). This infrastructure does not erase domestic censorship, but it creates alternative routes for films that may be difficult to circulate locally.

*Facing Mirrors* demonstrates the value of a dual circulation model. It received domestic attention through its Tehran release, including discussion on state media, and international recognition through festivals. The distributor lists the Montreal World Film Festival, Frameline, Outfest, the Washington DC International Film Festival, the Paris Gay & Lesbian Film Festival, and the Austin Gay and Lesbian Film Festival. Ajam’s account claims awards and nominations at more than sixty-four LGBTQ and international festivals, while the official distributor lists several specific honors ([The Film Collaborative](https://www.thefilmcollaborative.org/films/facingmirrors); [Ajam Media Collective](https://ajammc.com/2013/05/11/queer-and-trans-subjects-in-iranian-cinema-between-representation-agency-and-orientalist-fantasies/)). These are strong indicators of festival circulation, but they are not a systematic audience study.

Turkish activist documentaries often depend on transnational funding and partnership. *Proudly Trans in Turkey* received support from Istanbul LGBTT, Pembe Hayat, Amnesty International Turkey, the Human Resource Development Foundation, and the Consulate of the Netherlands. *Trans X Istanbul* was developed within the Transxturkey multimedia project, supported through European human-rights funding and Turkish partner organizations. The production history of *Trans X* also makes visible the risks of participation: several planned subjects declined because their families might see the film.

In Arab cinema, international funding can enable films that would otherwise be impossible to produce or exhibit, while also provoking accusations that queer representation is a Western invention. Maria Abdel Karim notes that many Middle Eastern films about homosexuality have been funded or co-produced by Western institutions. Her discussion of *Circumstance* shows how Maryam Keshavarz filmed in Lebanon after disguising the film’s subject from local authorities; the film was banned in Iran and the Middle East but won the Sundance Audience Award in 2011. This evidence concerns lesbian representation rather than trans cinema, but it clarifies the broader political economy in which trans and queer films circulate.

Digital distribution creates further possibilities. Human Rights Watch reported that Aflamuna’s 2020 online program “Love and Identity in Arab Cinema” brought queer Arab films to audiences during Pride month, allowing viewers to access films outside official theatrical restrictions ([Younes](https://www.hrw.org/news/2020/06/26/aflamuna-film-festival-amplifies-queer-voices-in-arab-cinema)). Digital circulation can bypass censorship, but it cannot eliminate surveillance, unequal internet access, platform moderation, or the danger that visibility creates for subjects and families.

## Trans theory: embodiment, recognition, and regional specificity

### Performativity is not performance

Judith Butler’s account of gender performativity describes gender as an effect of repeated, socially regulated acts. The point is not that individuals freely choose gender as a theatrical role. Rather, norms become naturalized through repetition, and the body becomes intelligible through those norms. The influential summary of Butler’s work through drag emphasizes that drag exposes gender’s imitative structure by showing that there is no original gender behind the performance ([“Realness as Resistance”](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/hypatia/article/realness-as-resistance-queer-feminism-neoliberalism-and-early-trans-critiques-of-butler/3552DB67342DCAF62C7C040C41F88A73)).

This distinction matters because a trans person is not simply “performing” a gender in the same sense that a drag performer stages one. *Facing Mirrors* dramatizes this distinction when Eddy attempts to use his brother’s driving license. His attempt to become legible to the Guidance Patrol is a tactical act of passing, but the film does not imply that his identity is a disguise. The state officer’s inability to read him is a problem of institutional recognition, not proof that Eddy is inauthentic.

The danger of reducing transgender life to performativity is identified by Jay Prosser. His account of transsexuality emphasizes the embodied, psychic, and social force of transition, including narratives of gender realness and the felt materiality of the body. Prosser’s critique of early Butlerian queer feminism is that strong claims about embodied gender can be treated as theoretically suspect or insufficiently anti-essentialist ([discussion of Prosser’s critique](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/hypatia/article/realness-as-resistance-queer-feminism-neoliberalism-and-early-trans-critiques-of-butler/3552DB67342DCAF62C7C040C41F88A73)). *Be Like Others* requires both perspectives: surgery can be a state-medical route to binary recognition, but it can also be desired as a material transformation that makes a person’s body more livable.

Susan Stryker’s work helps prevent the category from becoming too narrow. Transgender can name a broad field of bodily and social practices that disturb the assumption that gender follows naturally from sex. Stryker’s emphasis on “desubjugated knowledge” also insists that trans people produce knowledge about their own experiences; they are not merely objects for medical, legal, or cinematic interpretation. This principle is crucial for reading the testimony in *Be Like Others*, the self-positioning of Eddy in *Facing Mirrors*, and Ebru’s activist authority in *Trans X Istanbul*.

### Medicalization and the politics of recognition

Viviane Namaste’s critique of queer theory redirects attention from abstract identity disruption to the institutional structures that make particular identities possible or impossible. A theory that celebrates fluidity while neglecting clinics, courts, employment, housing, and police practices risks reproducing the invisibility it claims to challenge ([discussion of Namaste](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/hypatia/article/realness-as-resistance-queer-feminism-neoliberalism-and-early-trans-critiques-of-butler/3552DB67342DCAF62C7C040C41F88A73)).

Iran’s medico-legal system makes this institutional dimension unmistakable. The pathway described by Saeidzadeh includes thirteen psychiatric sessions at the Tehran Institute of Psychiatry, referral to the Legal Medicine Organization, certification of Gender Identity Disorder, administrative-court permission, and the possibility of legal name and gender change after surgery. The process distinguishes applicants understood as “true” transsexuals from homosexual applicants, who may be redirected toward further psychotherapy. It therefore does not simply recognize an identity already present; it produces a legally intelligible subject through psychiatric, religious, and administrative procedures.

Nancy Fraser’s concept of misrecognition is particularly useful here. Misrecognition is not merely a bad attitude or an insulting representation. It is an institutional relation that denies people full participation in social life. Saeidzadeh applies this framework to Iranian trans people, arguing that the legal and medical system can permit surgery while still subordinating trans people’s status. The law may allow a procedure without recognizing the social rights, employment, family relations, reproduction, inheritance, or citizenship claims of the person who undergoes it.

This distinction clarifies the apparent contradiction at the center of *Be Like Others*. Surgery may offer access to identification documents, family negotiation, employment, safety, and social legibility. At the same time, it may be required through a pathologizing system that treats gender variance as illness and homosexuality as an impermissible alternative. The film’s subjects are neither simply coerced victims nor unambiguously liberated consumers of medical technology. They negotiate a constrained field in which surgery may be both an instrument of survival and a demand imposed by the state’s binary order.

Najmabadi’s historical work complicates the idea that the Iranian state simply “forces” trans people into surgery. She emphasizes activist agency, local debates, and the ways that legal legibility has sometimes opened livable spaces. Saeidzadeh’s fieldwork likewise shows that many trans people reject the diagnosis of disorder while strategically using medical authority to gain family acceptance and access to services. These positions are not mutually exclusive. A person may exercise agency within a coercive institution; agency does not make the institution non-coercive.

### Local concepts and decolonial translation

Sahin Acikgoz argues that the transnational circulation of “transgender” can reveal a convergence between modernization and epistemological colonization. When an Anglophone umbrella term is treated as universally transparent, it may erase religious, class-based, ethnic, and racial particularities. Acikgoz’s case studies include *Be Like Others*, *Proudly Trans in Turkey*, Pınar Selek’s *Maskeler, Süvariler, Gacılar*, and Bülent Ersoy, and bring Turkish and Persian traditions into dialogue with English, Spanish, and Portuguese contexts ([Acikgoz](https://hdl.handle.net/2027.42/163292)).

This does not mean that “transgender” should never be used for MENA subjects. It means that the term should remain historically and politically accountable. The category may be useful for comparison, activism, festival programming, and scholarship, but it cannot replace local histories of gender, kinship, religion, medicine, class, or law.

Katrina Roen’s critique of the whiteness of transgender theory is also relevant, even though her empirical examples concern Indigenous South Pacific communities rather than MENA. Roen argues that some gender-liminal people resist Western medical discourses in order to maintain cultural values and that trans theory must attend to racialized bodies and culturally specific ways of being ([Roen](https://doi.org/10.1080/09589230120086467)). Her methodological lesson can be applied cautiously to MENA cinema: neither resistance to surgery nor pursuit of surgery should automatically be translated into a universal Western political narrative.

Najmabadi’s history of Iranian gender and sexuality further warns against projecting contemporary binary categories backward. Persian terms and practices such as *amrad* and *mukhannas* belonged to historical arrangements that cannot simply be renamed “transgender” or “gay.” The same caution applies to the early Iranian cross-dressing films discussed by Bassiri and to Arab cinematic performances of gender disguise.

### Intersectionality and the material body

Intersectionality is not an optional addition to trans analysis. Gender is mediated by class, religion, nationality, ethnicity, race, age, family position, migration status, and access to institutions. The MENA transnational feminist scholarship emphasizes that borders are gendered, sexualized, and racialized, and that their effects differ across populations ([“Transnational feminist approaches”](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/25785273.2023.2231775)).

In *Facing Mirrors*, Eddy’s wealthy family and passport access contrast with Rana’s debt, imprisoned husband, and precarious taxi labor. In *Be Like Others*, the clinic connects surgery to employment, housing, family authority, and the ability to remain Iranian. In *Trans X Istanbul*, trans identity is inseparable from urban redevelopment, sex work, police inaction, family rejection, refugee vulnerability, and access to education. These are not background variables. They determine which bodies can move, which identities can be recognized, and which forms of self-presentation become dangerous.

## Film theory: representation, gaze, genre, and documentary form

### Representation and the gaze

Film does not simply reflect a pre-existing trans identity. It organizes visibility through framing, narrative perspective, editing, genre, voice, performance, and circulation. Representation decides who is introduced as a subject, who is interpreted as a problem, who is granted interiority, and who is made available for the viewer’s curiosity.

Laura Mulvey’s account of the male gaze remains important because it identifies how classical narrative cinema organizes visual pleasure around an active, usually masculine spectator and a feminized object of looking. But MENA trans cinema requires a more plural account of spectatorship. Jackie Stacey argues that female spectators can make multiple identifications across gender boundaries and that homoerotic pleasures should not be excluded from feminist film theory. Maria Abdel Karim applies this insight to *Caramel*, where close-ups, tactile hair washing, and reciprocal looks construct a lesbian gaze rather than a conventional male-centered spectacle.

Trans spectatorship requires a further extension. A trans character can be represented as an object of curiosity, a victim, a medical case, an activist, a comic disguise, or a desiring subject. A film can invite cisgender spectators to identify with a trans character without guaranteeing trans agency or trans reception. It can also make the viewer experience the pressure of recognition: the viewer knows the character’s identity while other characters, institutions, or cameras do not.

The Orientalist gaze complicates this further. Some international audiences have historically consumed MENA queer and trans subjects as evidence of religious backwardness, authoritarian cruelty, or exotic difference. Ajam Media Collective argues that *Facing Mirrors* disrupted an Orientalist expectation by offering an Iranian trans protagonist whose agency and local production challenged the kind of Middle Eastern queer narrative more readily welcomed by Western media. This is a valuable interpretation, but it remains a particular critical argument rather than a general measurement of Western reception.

### Genre and cinematic space

Genre shapes what a trans story can mean. A family drama tends to organize gender around intimacy, kinship, and recognition. A clinic documentary organizes it around diagnosis, waiting, testimony, and medical authority. An activist documentary organizes it around public space, collective action, evidence, and political address.

*Facing Mirrors* borrows from the road movie and thriller without becoming a conventional thriller. The escape from a forced marriage provides suspense, but the film redirects that suspense toward the developing relationship between Rana and Eddy. *Be Like Others* uses the clinic as a narrative center, making waiting rooms, medical consultations, and public Tehran part of a social anatomy. *Trans X Istanbul* moves across neighborhoods, demolished buildings, demonstrations, family homes, and protest spaces, turning the city itself into an archive of structural violence.

Theories of accented and diasporic cinema clarify how space can carry displacement. Hamid Naficy identifies exilic and diasporic films through multilingualism, return narratives, border consciousness, and interstitial production. Laura Marks’s account of haptic visuality emphasizes the sensory and embodied dimensions of intercultural cinema. De Man, however, warns against treating these formal qualities as automatic consequences of filmmaker biography. They should be analyzed in relation to production, subject matter, circulation, and spectatorship rather than used as ethnic labels.

### Documentary ethics and modes

Documentary is not transparent access to reality. Bill Nichols’s modes—expository, observational, interactive, and reflexive—are useful precisely because they show how documentaries construct knowledge. Çakırlar identifies all four in *Trans X Istanbul*. The film uses expository voice-over and political information, observational footage of conflict and demonstrations, interactive exchanges between Binder and Ebru, and reflexive acknowledgment of the filmmaker’s position.

Documentary ethics therefore involve more than whether a filmmaker has good intentions. They involve consent, selection, editing, access, audience, funding, circulation, and the possibility that visibility may expose subjects to harm. Pooja Rangan’s critique of the “documentary logic of sobriety” warns that humanitarian seriousness can subordinate aesthetic and political complexity to the urgent display of suffering. Cüneyt Çakırlar applies a related concern to transnational LGBTQ documentaries, arguing that globally legible victimhood can obscure regional political differences and reproduce the “saviour” logic of the Gay International.

Relational approaches offer a useful counterpoint. Jørgen Nåls argues that intercultural documentary can create a shared “third culture” through relational empathy and that informed consent must be understood as an ongoing process rather than a single signature ([Nåls](https://doi.org/10.18546/fej.01.2.06)). *Trans X Istanbul* approaches this ideal through its visible relationship between Binder and Ebru, though the film cannot eliminate the asymmetry between an outsider filmmaker and a local activist. In *Be Like Others*, the available sources do not provide sufficient evidence about consent procedures, participant review, or later audience effects. An ethical analysis must therefore identify the stakes without claiming facts not documented.

## Case study: *Facing Mirrors* (Iran, 2011)

### Synopsis and production context

*Facing Mirrors* is often described as the first Iranian narrative film to feature a transgender protagonist. The Film Collaborative presents it as the first narrative film from Iran centered on a transgender main character; Ajam Media Collective describes it more strongly as the first film written, produced, and screened in Iran with a female-to-male transgender main character ([The Film Collaborative](https://www.thefilmcollaborative.org/films/facingmirrors); [Ajam Media Collective](https://ajammc.com/2013/05/11/queer-and-trans-subjects-in-iranian-cinema-between-representation-agency-and-orientalist-fantasies/)). Because these are promotional and critical descriptions rather than a complete national film history, the safest conclusion is that the film represents a major first in the documented history of Iranian narrative cinema.

Directed by Negar Azarbayjani and produced by Fereshteh Taerpour, both cisgender women according to Ajam’s account, the film follows Adineh, who calls himself Eddy, and Rana. Eddy is wealthy, rebellious, and waiting for a passport that will allow him to leave Iran for female-to-male surgery in Germany. His father wants to marry him to a male cousin. Rana is a conservative wife and mother who drives a taxi because her husband is imprisoned and the family needs money to pay his debt. Their encounter creates an unlikely friendship across class, religious, and ethical differences. The official synopsis describes the relationship as developing despite social norms and religious beliefs ([The Film Collaborative](https://www.thefilmcollaborative.org/films/facingmirrors)).

The production context is therefore crucial. The film does not present a generic “Iranian trans experience.” It places a trans man within a family possessing wealth and mobility, and a cisgender woman within economic precarity and patriarchal obligation. Eddy’s access to a passport and possible surgery abroad contrasts with Rana’s need to drive a taxi in a social environment where women doing so is taboo for her class. Their relationship is not based on identical oppression; it is built through an encounter between different forms of constraint.

### Passing, recognition, and the road

The film’s narrative is structured around movement. Eddy is waiting to leave the country, Rana is driving because she cannot remain economically stationary, and the friendship develops through a taxi journey that becomes an improvised route away from family control. The road is not simply a symbol of freedom. It is also a space of surveillance, police intervention, and exposure.

The Guidance Patrol sequence makes the politics of legibility explicit. When police stop Eddy and a female friend, he tries unsuccessfully to pass his brother’s driving license as his own. The scene gives Eddy tactical agency: he does not passively accept the officer’s interpretation but attempts to manipulate the available bureaucratic sign. His failure shows how gender is institutionally read through documents, appearance, and bodily assumptions. The scene does not prove that Eddy is “really” a man only after surgery; it shows that the state demands a coherent alignment between identity, document, and visible body.

Butler’s theory helps explain the scene’s repetition of gender norms, while Prosser and Namaste prevent the analysis from reducing it to a playful performance. Eddy’s use of the license is a performance in the narrow sense of a strategic act, but his desire for surgery and his relation to his body are not equivalent to disguise. The police encounter exposes the difference between a person’s lived identity and the administrative demand that identity become immediately recognizable.

A bathroom scene provides a counter-space. After the public confrontation, Eddy cries alone, and the film makes visible the pain and loneliness concealed by his defiance. The bathroom is not an uncomplicated private refuge: it is a gendered space in which bodies are expected to appear intelligible. Yet it permits a temporary release from the public role that Eddy has just performed. The sequence moves from institutional confrontation to embodied affect, connecting recognition to vulnerability rather than treating passing as a successful solution.

The film’s escape structure also modifies the thriller. An Australian review observes that the attempt to escape the father’s wedding plans creates narrative tension, but that Azarbayjani largely avoids thriller conventions in order to explore what the two protagonists share as people willing to resist social convention ([SBS review](https://www.sbs.com.au/whats-on/article/facing-mirrors-review/g29ypkxgm)). The film thus uses suspense without allowing the trans character to become merely a plot device. The question is not only whether Eddy will escape marriage; it is whether two people with different class positions can produce solidarity without erasing their differences.

### Religion, class, and agency

Rana is described as traditional and religious, but the film does not turn religious belief into a simple antagonist. Her actions are shaped by debt, marriage, family honor, and gendered labor as much as by doctrine. The friendship asks her to revise her understanding of Eddy, but it does not require her to become culturally or religiously indistinguishable from him.

This is important because international criticism often organizes MENA queer stories around a binary between secular liberation and religious repression. *Facing Mirrors* instead shows that a woman’s ability to work, move, and make decisions is also constrained by class and family. Rana’s taxi driving is itself a gendered transgression. Eddy’s trans identity becomes legible to her through an encounter that changes the meaning of the person she has already begun to help.

The cross-class structure also complicates the idea that trans recognition is solely a matter of personal identity. Eddy’s family can use marriage, mobility, and economic power to constrain him. Rana has fewer resources but gains a form of mobility through paid labor. Their solidarity emerges because each recognizes the other’s struggle, yet the film does not suggest that they occupy the same social position.

Fraser’s status model of recognition is useful here. Eddy seeks more than emotional acceptance from his father; he seeks the status of a full participant in family and social life. Rana also seeks status: as a wife whose husband is imprisoned, a mother responsible for household survival, and a woman whose labor is treated as socially improper. The film’s political force lies in placing these struggles in relation rather than ranking one as more authentic.

### The gaze and the problem of authorship

The film also intervenes in the transnational gaze. Ajam contrasts the local reception of *Facing Mirrors* with the international attention given to Maryam Keshavarz’s *Circumstance*, which was shot in Lebanon and uses an American-accented Persian according to the critique. Ajam argues that *Circumstance* fit Western Orientalist expectations more easily, while *Facing Mirrors* disrupted them by emerging from Iranian production and by giving its trans character agency. This argument should be treated as a critical interpretation rather than a generalizable audience finding, but it identifies a real representational problem: international circuits do not distribute all MENA queer films equally.

The film’s authorship nevertheless raises ethical questions. The principal filmmakers were cisgender women, and the film’s historical importance may encourage audiences to treat it as an authentic voice of Iranian trans life. That would confuse representational significance with community authorship. The film can offer a sympathetic and complex narrative while still being shaped by cisgender creative decisions, genre conventions, and festival expectations.

A trans-theoretical reading should therefore hold two judgments together. First, *Facing Mirrors* gives Eddy narrative agency and refuses to make his body a medical spectacle. Second, it remains a mediated representation whose authority cannot be established simply by the fact that it is Iranian. The film’s local production challenges the Orientalist expectation that MENA subjects require Western explanation, but national origin alone does not guarantee ethical representation.

### Reception and limits

The film received the Special Jury Crystal Simorgh at Iran’s 29th Fajr International Film Festival and numerous international festival honors. The Film Collaborative lists a Jury Award for Best Film at the 2011 Montreal World Film Festival, a Jury Award for Best Feature at Frameline, a Grand Prix at the Paris Gay & Lesbian Film Festival, and Best Narrative Feature at the Austin Gay and Lesbian Film Festival. Another account identifies a Best First Feature award at Frameline in 2012 ([The Film Collaborative](https://www.thefilmcollaborative.org/films/facingmirrors); [Habibi](https://yris.yira.org/campus/facing-mirrors-a-film-about-transgender-rights-in-iran/)). The differing descriptions of the Frameline honor do not alter the broader finding that the film circulated successfully through international LGBTQ and general film festivals.

The Guardian’s report on the 2012 Tehran release is especially important because it documents a domestic public effect: the film gave Iranian television and radio a reason to discuss transsexuality, and young trans viewers reportedly encouraged others to watch it. These accounts show both domestic and international reception, but they do not provide systematic audience numbers, demographic data, or long-term evidence of social change.

The film’s principal limitation in this paper is evidentiary. A fully retrievable peer-reviewed close reading and a complete censorship and distribution history were not available in the supplied material. The interpretation above therefore combines the film’s official synopsis, reviews, critical commentary, and documented scenes rather than claiming a comprehensive archival account.

## Case study: *Be Like Others* (Iran, 2008)

### The clinic and the contradiction

Tanaz Eshaghian’s *Be Like Others* is a documentary about Iranian trans people navigating a medical and legal process that links gender-affirming surgery to social and civic recognition. Its opening establishes the governing contradiction through two statements on a black screen: sex-change operations are legal in the Islamic Republic, while homosexuality is punishable by death. The film then moves to the Mirdamad Surgical Center, where Paris-trained surgeon Bahram Mir-Jalali sees applicants on designated days and performs government-approved operations ([IranNamag](https://www.irannamag.com/en/article/queering-iranian-nation-like-others-resistance-heteronormative-nationalism/)).

The black screen is formally significant. It does not begin with an individual face or a personal story; it begins with a juridical opposition. The viewer is asked to understand trans life through the relationship between two state categories: a permitted medical intervention and a criminalized sexual identity. The film’s first act therefore frames the body as a site where law, religion, medicine, and national self-representation meet.

The clinic becomes the documentary’s principal social space. It is neither a neutral hospital nor merely a place of healing. It is a gatekeeping institution where bodies are examined, identities are named, and applicants learn the terms under which they may become recognizable. The film’s attention to waiting rooms, consultations, doctors, families, and psychiatric evaluation transforms medical procedure into a drama of citizenship.

The available sources describe a four- to six-month process of psychological and medical therapies, including physical examinations, hormonal treatment, and psychological evaluation. Saeidzadeh’s socio-legal research describes a related pathway involving thirteen psychiatric sessions at the Tehran Institute of Psychiatry, referral to the Legal Medicine Organization, diagnosis, and judicial authorization. These accounts should not be treated as identical measures: one describes the documentary’s narrative of filtering, while the other describes a fieldwork-based administrative process.

### Documentary form and the national image

The film repeatedly places intimate testimony against public images of Tehran. The viewer sees chador-clad women, traffic, skyscrapers, murals of Khomeini and Khamenei, revolutionary heroes, and Iran-Iraq war martyrs. IranNamag interprets this juxtaposition as a contrast between the state’s idealized images of pious masculinity and femininity and the intimate lives of trans people whose bodies do not fit the national image.

The urban images perform more than contextual work. They make the city an ideological landscape. The clinic is not outside the nation; it is surrounded by the signs through which the nation imagines itself. The documentary’s movement between public murals and private conversations demonstrates how gender norms are distributed through architecture, media, family, medicine, and law.

Minoo Moallem’s concept of filmic space as a site of cultural struggle is useful here. The documentary’s camera enters a space that official Iranian nationalism attempts to organize through binary gender, religious virtue, and family continuity. Yet the film does not simply oppose private authenticity to public ideology. The subjects want to remain in Iran, to work, marry, receive documents, and live among family and neighbors. Their political demand is not necessarily exile or Western rescue; it is the possibility of belonging without the erasure of complexity.

The film’s institutional framing has been read in two conflicting ways. Joanne Kouyoumjian’s review emphasizes the striking fact that surgery is legal and available, and it argues that the documentary does not treat the Iranian regime as uniquely Islamic. Instead, it places the procedure within a broader history of medicine and the pathologization of homosexuality and gender confusion ([Kouyoumjian, “Gender Neutralized”](https://reverseshot.org/symposiums/entry/167/be_others)). Boroujerdi emphasizes the state’s treatment of sexual and gender difference as illness and the way the clinic reproduces a hierarchy between homosexual and transsexual identities ([Boroujerdi](https://doi.org/10.20935/al321)). These readings are not contradictory. The film can show the historical complexity of medicalization while also exposing its coercive effects.

### Surgery as agency and constraint

The documentary’s participants do not speak with one voice. The available criticism identifies Vida and Anoosh as appearing satisfied with surgery, while Ali faces severe consequences from social rejection. Other participants hesitate, postpone, or say that they would not choose surgery if the surrounding legal and social conditions were different. Near the end of the film, two trans women say that they would have refused surgery if they had not been in Iran or had known that the process would sever their family ties ([IranNamag](https://www.irannamag.com/en/article/queering-iranian-nation-like-others-resistance-heteronormative-nationalism/)).

These statements make surgery a problem of constrained agency. A narrow liberal reading might define freedom as the ability to refuse medical transition. A narrow state reading might define freedom as the ability to receive surgery and new documents. The film demonstrates that both choices are shaped by family, law, employment, violence, and national belonging.

Prosser’s emphasis on embodied gender realness helps explain why the participants may desire surgery without accepting the state’s diagnosis. Surgery can be materially meaningful even when the medical category that authorizes it is rejected. Butler’s performativity, meanwhile, clarifies how the state produces a binary subject through repeated examinations, documents, dress codes, and legal procedures. Namaste’s institutional critique shows why neither individual identity nor discursive subversion is sufficient: the clinic, court, family, and workplace determine the practical consequences of being recognized.

The film also shows how medicalization can be strategically appropriated. Saeidzadeh’s interviews indicate that Iranian trans people may reject the idea that they suffer from a disorder while relying on medical authority to persuade families, obtain documents, or gain access to surgery. Medical language becomes a resource because it is one of the few languages the state and family recognize. The result is not a simple false consciousness. It is an unstable negotiation in which a pathologizing institution can be used to create a more livable life.

### Homosexuality, transsexuality, and the state

The documentary’s opening contrast between legal surgery and criminalized homosexuality is not merely a revelation of hypocrisy. It shows how the Iranian state constructs different categories of sexual and gendered life. Iranian authorities have historically treated transsexuality as a correctable medical anomaly while treating homosexuality as a criminal or moral offense. Critics quoted in the Guardian argue that this distinction has pressured some gay and lesbian people who do not identify as transgender to consider surgery. Other scholars, especially Najmabadi, emphasize that trans activists and trans people themselves helped produce a distinct legal category that could offer protection in a hostile environment.

The film’s treatment of Vida is especially complex. A review describes her as a postoperative trans woman who counsels applicants and repeats the official claim that homosexuality is a disorder corrected by “straightening out” gender. The reviewer increasingly sees her as a government mouthpiece. Yet the film’s inclusion of her testimony also reveals how state discourse can be inhabited, repeated, and modified by people whose own lives are shaped by it. A trans subject can criticize homosexuality, defend surgery, and still be subordinated by the same institutions she appears to represent.

This is where Saeidzadeh’s account of misrecognition becomes more useful than a simple opposition between state and subject. Legal recognition of surgery does not necessarily recognize trans people as full social participants. Indeed, a system that distinguishes “real” transsexuals from homosexuals may produce hierarchies among trans people, stigmatize trans women, and reproduce homophobia as the price of recognition.

The documentary also links gender to class and livelihood. IranNamag’s account describes subjects who need surgery or legal recognition to gain access to work, education, housing, dignity, and safety. It also discusses post-operative economic precarity and sex work. These details prevent the film from being read as a story about identity alone. The question is not simply “Who am I?” but “Under what conditions can I work, remain housed, maintain family relations, and be treated as a citizen?”

### The transnational documentary address

Eshaghian is an Iranian-born American filmmaker, and the film speaks simultaneously to Iranian and international audiences. This transnational address has political advantages: it makes the Iranian state’s contradictions visible to viewers who may know little about local legal and religious debates. It also risks producing an exceptionalist narrative in which Iran is consumed as a paradoxical spectacle—an Islamic state that permits surgery yet represses homosexuality.

Acikgoz’s decolonial analysis helps identify this danger. A film can challenge the Iranian government’s narrative while still being absorbed into a Euro-American knowledge system that expects Iranian trans people to serve as evidence of either Islamic cruelty or liberal modernity. IranNamag’s discussion of whiteness and “modern” recognition emphasizes that the film’s circulation can place subjects within a global hierarchy of intelligibility.

At the same time, the film resists a purely external gaze by allowing subjects to articulate why they want to remain in Iran. The desire to stay is not necessarily evidence of false consciousness or nationalism. It is a claim to home, language, family, history, and citizenship. The documentary’s most powerful moments occur when its subjects refuse the assumption that emancipation must mean departure.

### Ethics and reception

The available evidence is stronger for the film’s critical interpretation than for its production ethics. Sources describe the clinic, participants, and family relationships in detail, but the retrieved records do not document consent procedures, participant review, later objections, or the consequences of international circulation. It would therefore be unjustified to claim either that the film exploited its subjects or that it fully resolved the ethical problems of documentary exposure.

The formal risks are nevertheless clear. The clinic setting can make trans people appear as medical cases. The opening legal contradiction can turn their lives into evidence of national paradox. The international viewer may be invited to marvel at the availability of surgery while overlooking the subjects’ ordinary demands for employment, family life, and safety. Conversely, the film’s sustained attention to divergent testimonies prevents a single interpretation from becoming complete.

Reception evidence includes substantial criticism and festival circulation, but no reliable aggregate audience data were supplied. The film’s distribution history, domestic reception, and participant responses after release therefore remain partially unavailable. The strongest supported judgment is that *Be Like Others* made Iranian trans-medical politics internationally visible while leaving unresolved the ethical and political question of how that visibility is used.

## Case study: *Trans X Istanbul* (Turkey, 2014)

### From individual life to urban system

*Trans X Istanbul* is directed by Maria Binder and her mother, both of whom had moved from Germany to Turkey. The film follows Ebru Kırancı, an Istanbul-based trans activist, through struggles involving hate crimes, urban displacement, family rejection, sex work, and political organizing. It formed part of the Transxturkey multiplatform project, which sought to increase visibility and support equal rights for trans people. The film premiered at the Istanbul Film Festival and continued to circulate through Documentarist Istanbul Documentary Days ([Altyazı interview](https://www.transxistanbul.com/pdf/altyazi_en.pdf); [Trans X Istanbul official site](http://transxistanbul.com/index_en.php)).

The production began in 2009 with the intention of following four people. Most declined because they feared that their families might see the film. Binder therefore centered Ebru and describes the result as a personal film seen through Ebru’s eyes. She explicitly says that the film does not seek objectivity at every moment and that she excluded neighbors’ arguments because she was not making a conventional news documentary ([Altyazı](https://www.transxistanbul.com/pdf/altyazi_en.pdf)).

This production history is not a minor anecdote. It determines the film’s form. The film is not a survey of a representative community, because the subjects who refused participation are absent. Nor is Ebru simply an informant chosen by an invisible filmmaker. She becomes the film’s organizing intelligence, directing attention toward places, conflicts, and histories that she wants documented.

### Nichols’s modes and the collaborative gaze

Çakırlar identifies four documentary modes in *Trans X Istanbul*: expository, observational, interactive, and reflexive. The film uses explanatory voice-over and political information; observational footage of demonstrations and neighborhood conflict; interactive encounters between Binder, Ebru, and other participants; and reflexive awareness of the filmmaker’s outsider position ([Çakırlar](https://irep.ntu.ac.uk/id/eprint/31902/1/9389_Cakirlar.pdf)).

The combination of modes allows the film to move between personal testimony and structural analysis. Ebru’s story is not isolated from the city. The film connects transphobic speech to eviction, urban redevelopment, police inaction, medical neglect, legal ambiguity, and labor exclusion. In the Avcılar sequence, the neighbors’ language escalates from opposition to prostitution, to rejection of trans people, to physical attacks with sticks. The progression makes visible how hate speech can become hate crime when institutions fail to intervene ([Altyazı](https://www.transxistanbul.com/pdf/altyazi_en.pdf)).

The film’s urban form is therefore political. Istanbul appears not as an exotic postcard but as a contested landscape. The contrast between demolished buildings, construction sites, idealized city images, and trans residents’ precarious homes makes urban redevelopment part of the production of gendered violence. Çakırlar connects Tarlabaşı’s transformation to the displacement of poor and transient populations, including trans people. Relocation to the city’s peripheries can intensify exposure to violence by removing residents from established networks and familiar spaces.

The film’s perspective also moves across scales. It begins with community violence in urban districts, turns toward Ebru’s family history in Zonguldak, and later incorporates the Gezi Park protests and Istanbul Pride. This movement prevents trans identity from being reduced either to private trauma or to abstract activism. Family, neighborhood, city, and national politics become connected systems.

### Ebru’s activism and the politics of labor

Ebru’s testimony links gender to class and work. In a 2014 interview, she describes using the E-5 highway for sex work, being unable to attend university after high school, and believing that state policy leaves trans people with few occupational choices. She distinguishes between people who choose sex work and those forced into it, insisting that the problem is structural rather than a moral defect ([Altyazı](https://www.transxistanbul.com/pdf/altyazi_en.pdf)).

This distinction matters because Turkish film and media have often represented trans women primarily through prostitution, violence, and alienation. Saruhan’s critique shows how even sympathetic films can reproduce that pattern. *Trans X Istanbul* responds by making sex work part of a broader political economy rather than a defining essence. Ebru is an activist, organizer, worker, friend, and political thinker. Her history of sex work does not exhaust her identity.

The film’s official materials describe thousands of trans women living in Turkey’s major cities, increasing murders, and failures to investigate hate crimes. These figures and generalizations come from promotional material and should not be treated as an independent statistical study. They nevertheless identify the political problem the film addresses: formal visibility does not guarantee investigation, prosecution, or protection ([Trans X Istanbul official site](http://transxistanbul.com/index_en.php)).

The film also connects trans exclusion to migration. A later report on Binder’s work describes efforts to establish a trans refugee home in Turkey, with many LGBT refugees arriving from Syria and trans people in camps facing especially severe abuse and harassment ([Dawn](https://images.dawn.com/news/1175176/everywhere-they-go-they-are-expelled-filmmaker-discusses-plight-of-trans-community-in-turkey)). This material broadens the film’s national frame, although it should not be assumed that the refugee issue is fully represented within the original 2014 film.

### Recognition without surgery

Unlike *Be Like Others*, *Trans X Istanbul* does not organize its narrative around medical transition. Its central question is not how a trans person becomes legally legible through surgery but how trans people survive and organize under conditions of institutional abandonment. Binder’s account of Turkish identity cards—blue or pink, with a pink card requiring gender-reassignment surgery—shows that medicalization remains part of legal recognition, but the film’s political energy comes from collective action rather than the clinic.

This difference illuminates two models of recognition. In Iran, surgery can operate as a route to documents and status, even when it is pathologizing. In Turkey, the issue is more visibly connected to public space, policing, employment, violence, and activist solidarity. The contrast should not be overstated: Turkish trans people also face medical and legal gatekeeping, while Iranian trans people also build activist networks. The films foreground different institutional problems rather than representing two completely separate social worlds.

Ebru’s activism also complicates the assumption that the most important political subject is the individual who successfully passes within the gender binary. Her work is collective and spatial. She helps residents respond to eviction, confront neighbors, document violence, and imagine forms of community care. The official synopsis’s account of a proposed retirement home for trans people points toward an alternative infrastructure of aging and belonging, although the promotional material does not document its completion.

### Transnational production and the savior gaze

The film’s German-Turkish production context generates ethical possibility and risk. Maria Binder and her mother moved from Germany to Turkey; the film was produced through transnational networks and circulated through international festivals. Such conditions can provide funding and audiences unavailable within a precarious national film economy. They can also make local activists valuable as internationally intelligible symbols of suffering and resistance.

Çakırlar’s central concept is the “transnational gaze,” which can reproduce the savior discourses of the Gay International. The problem is not simply that a foreign filmmaker represents a local subject. It is that global circulation may reward narratives that translate complex regional activism into a universal story of victimhood and liberation. The film’s visible collaboration with Ebru counters this danger: Ebru addresses Binder, directs attention, and appears as a political agent. Yet collaboration does not eliminate asymmetry. The filmmaker controls selection, editing, narration, and circulation.

The participants who declined to appear also matter. Their refusal is an active form of agency, but it creates a representational dilemma: the film’s visibility depends on the absence of people whose family risks may have been greater than Ebru’s or differently structured. The ethical question is therefore not whether the film should have included them against their wishes. It is how the film’s singular focus may be read as representative when its production history demonstrates that access was uneven.

Çakırlar also observes that the film could have addressed more of the internal conflicts within trans activism rather than presenting a globally legible struggle against transphobia. This criticism does not negate the film’s value. It identifies the tension between coalition-building and self-critique. An activist documentary may need a clear public argument, while a critical community documentary might need to show disagreement, hierarchy, and exclusion within the movement.

### Reception and limitations

*Trans X Istanbul* premiered at the Istanbul Film Festival, continued through Documentarist, and circulated as part of a broader activist platform. Its reception evidence is primarily official project material, interviews, and Çakırlar’s scholarly analysis. No systematic audience research or comparative domestic/international reception study was supplied.

The film’s strongest achievement is formal and political at once: it makes the urban production of trans vulnerability visible while preserving Ebru’s capacity to act. Its main limitation is not a failure of sympathy but the unresolved problem of scale. Ebru’s story becomes a vehicle for representing a community, a city, and a transnational political issue. The film acknowledges this process, but its international circulation may still encourage audiences to treat Istanbul as a case study in generalized trans oppression rather than as a site of specific classed, historical, and political struggles.

## Comparative synthesis

### Three films, three institutional formations

| Axis | *Facing Mirrors* | *Be Like Others* | *Trans X Istanbul* |
|---|---|---|---|
| Country and production | Iran; Iranian narrative feature by cisgender women | Iran; documentary by Iranian-born American filmmaker | Turkey; German-Turkish transnational documentary |
| Central form | Family drama with road and thriller elements | Clinic-centered observational and testimonial documentary | Activist documentary combining expository, observational, interactive, and reflexive modes |
| Trans subject | Eddy, a trans man seeking mobility and surgery abroad | Several Iranian trans people negotiating surgery, diagnosis, and recognition | Ebru Kırancı, trans activist and community organizer |
| Main institution | Family, marriage, police, passport, and class | Clinic, psychiatry, religious authority, judiciary, family, employment | Police, courts, urban redevelopment, family, labor, activist networks |
| Dominant political question | Can recognition and solidarity interrupt family and gendered obligation? | What does recognition mean when surgery is both survival and medicalization? | How does collective activism contest urban and structural violence? |

The three films do not offer a linear history from oppression to liberation. They reveal different ways that trans life becomes cinematic and political.

### Medical recognition and collective agency

In *Facing Mirrors*, medical transition is important but remains partly off-screen and transnational.
